title: The memory of the past
html_source:
The phrase “the memory of the past” alludes to a line in the song There Is a Flower That Bloometh in Wallace’s opera Maritana. The significance of references to “flowers”, and, of course, especially to “Bloometh” in the novel suggests a special significance to Joyce here. Perhaps it is to his lingering regrets for the turn his life took early on as he recreates it for Stephen in Portrait of the Artist. There on Sandymount Strand, the same setting as in Nausicaa, (“[Young Stephen] looked northward toward Howth,” the promontory the narrator mentions six times in Nausicaa), Stephen wonders, “Where is my boyhood now? Where was the soul that had hung back from her destiny, to brood alone upon the shame of her wounds and in her house of squalor and subterfuge… Or where was he?”

When Stephen is described in Portrait as “alone amidst… the veiled grey sunlight and gayclad figures of children and girls and voices and girlish in the air,” the similarities to Nausicaa could not be starker. The girl he is captivated by is described thusly: “Her long slender bare legs were delicate… Her thighs, fuller and soft-hued as ivory, were bared almost to the hips… Her slate-blue skirts were kilted boldly about her waist… But her long fair hair … touched, with wonder of mortal beauty, her face.” The narrator continues, “ She was… gazing out to sea; and when she felt his presence and the worship of his eyes, her eyes turned to him in quiet sufferance of his gaze…”

This moment radically transformed Stephen’s outlook, and led to a life of indulgence it is possible he came to deeply regret, and which may have contributed greatly to the sadness Gerty saw in Bloom’s face. That period of Stephen’s life, “[he] bore cynically with the shameful details of his secret riots in which he exulted to defile with patience whatever image had attracted his eyes.” Now, mature Bloom, despite whatever remorse he may feel, was about to defile the image that had attracted his eyes, the image he had nearly deified,with a secret, conscience-betraying act Stephen had habituated during, and despite, his virtue-seeking youth.
